newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia Gold-Royalty seen lowering profits.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia Gold-Royalty seen lowering profits.

text.p: A proposed gold royalty on miners in Western Australia, which produces most of Australia's gold, could shave off as much as A$11 an ounce in pre-tax profits based on the current price, analysts said on Thursday.

A post-tax levy of around 2.5 percent, as proposed this week by Western Australia state premier Richard Court, would cut profits by as much as A$7 an ounce using an average price of A$450 an ounce, Bell Securities resource analyst Keith Goode said in an industry report.
"There are also concerns that it could ultimately rise up to four to five percent of spot revenue," Goode said.
Moreover, say miners, the idea of a royalty comes as prices are low and ore grades are declining, boosting costs.
"It could not of come at a worse time," said Peter Lalor, managing director of Sons of Gwalia Ltd, one of Australia's largest gold mining companies.

"We had an eight-year low yesterday in the Australian dollar gold price ... we've got native title issues all over the place, the Australian dollar is out of control and we're mining lower and lower grades," Lalor said.
Gold currently fetches about A$448 an ounce, a level not seen since the late 1980s and down about A$100 from a year ago, although much of what miners produce is forward sold at much higher prices.
Australian miners have embraced forward selling more than any other country and imposition of a levy could only encourage more hedging, analysts said.
Only miners producing less than 1,000 ounces a year, would be exempt from the levy under the current propsoal.

"Every public company that's a producer produces more than 1,000 ounces," Lalor said. "This means the 25,000 ounce producer will pay the same as Sons of Gwalia at 500,000 ounces." Lalor, chairman of the gold industry forum comittee under the Chamber of Minerals and Energy of Western Australia Inc, said the state will be presented with the mining industry's reasons for opposing the levy sometime next week.

The submission is in response to remarks made by Court to reporters this week that the state was considering imposing a royalty of 1.25 percent of gold sale proceeds from January 1 next year, rising to 2.5 percent by July 1999.

Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) analyst Simon Middleton estimates some 30 percent of Australia's 1996/97 (July/June) gold production is sold forward at an average price of A$638 an ounce
For 1997/98, it is estimated that around 50 percent of Australia's production is sold forward at an average A$610 an ounce.
Unlike miners in other states, gold miners in Western Australia currently are exempt from paying royalties on gold although other metals are subject to royalties in that state.

Queensland has a 2.75 percent gross royalty, while in New South Wales a net smelter levy of four percent is equal to about a two percent gross royalty. The Northern Territory has an 18 percent net profit royalty.
Western Australia produces around 70 percent of the 300 tonnes or so of gold forecast to be produced in Australia this year.
